name: Gareth Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play electric bass in a theatre house band, record guide grooves for rehearsals and coach one young player. I earned a bachelor’s degree in music and have worked the pit for twenty-two years. I like the little nod from the drummer when we land a quiet ending together.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the theatre pay fit your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, our children are grown, and my partner has regular hours at a bus depot. We rent and have three months of expenses saved. My pay is typical for a working musician, with some other theatres nearby; a new pit seat still needs a real opening. I use AI sometimes for a set-list draft and then check it against the stage manager’s sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that quicker set-list drafts help if the signed call sheet still shows our pay. The drummer and I still have to hear when an actor holds a line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months saved and my partner’s regular wage make one late show fee manageable. I would still want written cancellation pay after last spring’s theatre leak moved two performances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would confirm eight paid shows and the young player’s lesson, then request a written cancellation clause. In the first year of mild AI I would keep playing and recording, using an occasional AI set-list draft only after checking each cue against the stage manager’s sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm while the signed shows and household wage hold. A delayed fee would annoy me, but it would not mean missing rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the leak cost the band?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre paid the rehearsal and postponed two performances. We waited six weeks for the replacement dates, so I want the fee rule on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you give the AI a rehearsal recording?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a set-list draft needs titles and times, not a singer’s voice. I keep the audio with the theatre.

say: I would accept **quicker set lists** if signed pay stays visible.
I would say **live bass playing** must follow an actor’s timing.
think: Our **three-month reserve** and partner wage cover one delayed show fee.
A **written cancellation clause** would settle the next moved performance.
do: Confirm **eight paid shows** and the pupil lesson this week.
Request **written cancellation pay** and check AI set-list drafts against the stage manager’s sheet.
feel: I feel **calm** while paid dates and household wages hold.
S0.quote: The drummer and I still have to hear when an actor holds a line.
fieldNote: His **experienced bass work** brings typical pay and three months of savings.
Occasional **AI set lists** are existing use, checked manually against signed theatre cues.

steps.text: Confirm eight paid theatre shows and one bass pupil lesson this week
Request written cancellation fee and check AI set lists against stage-manager sheet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that generated guide grooves could replace the recordings I make for cast rehearsal. I would ask for paid revision time in the next music call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guides provide about one fifth of my own pay. Losing them would hurt, though three months saved and my partner’s wage let me test a practical response.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total my guide invoices and ask for a paid sound-engineer demonstration of a new AI timing checker, which flags late bass notes in my own recording. In the first year I would try it only on a nameless track I own under the theatre’s paid-use licence and approved local storage, outside paid show hours; I would compare every mark by ear against the original and stop if it moves a note or the file leaves the theatre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a realistic cut to guide fees. A timing checker may save a retake, but it cannot book another show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put a cast member’s voice into the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, my bass alone is enough to test timing. A performer’s voice would need written permission and clear storage terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre should pay the engineer and the licence without taking a paid show hour from me. If it will not, I can keep marking the groove by ear.

say: I would warn **generated grooves** could replace my paid guides.
I would ask for **paid revision time** on the next theatre call.
think: The **guide recordings** supply one fifth of my pay.
Our **three-month reserve** gives some time to respond if orders fall.
do: Total **guide invoices** and request paid engineer demonstration outside paid shows.
Test **timing checker** after paid demo on owned nameless bass, theatre paid-use licence/local storage; compare by ear, stop errors/leakage.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a real threat to my guide fees.
S1.quote: A timing checker may save a retake, but it cannot book another show.
fieldNote: The **new AI lesson** needs paid instruction, theatre permission for paid use and no lost show hours.
The **manual comparison** and local storage protect cast audio and catch shifted notes.

steps.text: Total guide invoices and request paid engineer demo outside paid shows
Test after paid demo: owned nameless bass, paid-use licence/local storage; listen, stop errors/leakage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that thinking AGI by 2028 could make rehearsal grooves cheaply. Playing robots come around 2031, three years later, so our live bass calls have a different clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect guide orders to end in 2028, taking one fifth of my pay. I do not expect the theatre to replace the live band at once, but a run can close and leave a hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would total guide and show income, request a signed paid theatre season and ask for an actual pension estimate before considering retirement at sixty. In the first year after 2028, if paid live shows fall too, I would audition for a posted paid bass seat at another theatre only if the score is within my playing range, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the late bus works; I would keep this band and my pupil until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing a regular fifth of my own pay. Three months saved and some nearby theatres give me time, though no new seat is promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take any bass chair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A posted paid opening is only the start. I need to see the score, the actual travel cost and the last bus before making an audition trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop work at sixty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read a real pension estimate first. A birthday is not a signed show call or a wage.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 playing robots.
I would say **live bass calls** follow a different clock from guide tracks.
think: I expect **one-fifth of my pay** from guides to go in 2028.
A **closed theatre run** could worsen the gap, but is not my forecast.
do: Total **guide and show income**, request signed paid dates and an actual pension estimate now.
Audition for **posted paid bass seat** after 2028 live cuts only if playable, written net after travel replaces losses and bus fits.
Keep **current band and pupil** until a suitable signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a likely guide-fee loss with some search time.
S2.quote: A birthday is not a signed show call or a wage.
fieldNote: The expected **2028 guide loss** precedes 2031 playing robots, while live closures remain conditional.
A **different bass seat** needs posted paid work, playable score, after-travel replacement pay, bus and signed offer.

steps.text: Total guide/show income; request signed paid theatre season and actual pension estimate now
Audition for posted paid bass seat after live cuts if score playable and bus fits
Require written net after travel replacing losses; keep current band until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that five years until AGI by 2031 gives me time to learn amplifier repair on paid hours. Playing robots follow around 2034, after guide-making changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guide work may end by 2031. I know how a bass amp sounds when it is wrong, but I cannot open a live cabinet without training and supervision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I would check whether nearby repair shops accept a six-month amplifier-service certificate for paid assistant roles before enrolling. I would take an actual paid workshop place only if tuition is funded and weekly wages match any theatre hours it displaces. In the first year after 2031, if guide orders stop and paid shows shrink, I would seek a posted paid repair-assistant job only if that certificate qualifies, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses run after shifts; I would keep the band and pupil until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the workshop and a real job both pay. A certificate on its own cannot cover our flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you service an amp alone afterward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would work beside a qualified repair lead for the first checks. I would not touch live electrical parts alone until a signed safety assessment and the lead’s approval.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the workshop pays less than a show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid theatre calls and ask about another intake. Funded amplifier-repair tuition does not replace lost weekly wages.

say: I would say **five years** gives time to learn paid amplifier repair.
I would place **playing robots** around 2034, after guide-making changes.
think: The **guides may end** by 2031, while live shows could shrink too.
An **amp certificate** matters only if shops accept it and training pays.
do: Take **paid repair training** only if shops recognize certificate, tuition funded and wages match displaced theatre hours.
Seek **posted repair work** after 2031 guide/show cuts only if certificate qualifies, written net after travel replaces losses and buses fit.
Keep **band and pupil** until signed offer; work under lead until electrical safety approval.
feel: I feel **anxious** until both training and new work pay.
S3.quote: Funded amplifier-repair tuition does not replace lost weekly wages.
fieldNote: The **repair course** needs an accepted certificate, real paid place, funded tuition and unchanged weekly earnings.
The **repair job** needs a posted paid role, after-travel replacement net pay and supervised electrical work until sign-off.

steps.text: Take funded repair course only if shops accept certificate, place paid, displaced show wages matched
Seek posted repair job after guide/show cuts if certificate qualifies and late buses fit
Keep theatre/pupil until signed offer with written after-travel net replacing lost fees
Work under qualified repair lead until signed electrical safety approval

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that ten years until AGI by 2036 is time to ask what retirement really pays. Bass-playing robots follow around 2039; the band’s next signed show matters more today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might still want to play, and three months saved is not a retirement plan. I need an actual pension amount before I say how many shows I can leave behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request an actual pension estimate and save ten percent of each extra paid festival set after rent, food and bass repairs until we have five months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid theatre calls and my pupil while booked; if live show pay falls, I would apply for a posted paid arts-centre bass tutor role only if it still has funded in-person lesson hours, my music degree and pupil-coaching experience meet its requirements, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the late bus works. I would not leave the band until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about work that far ahead, but current calls and our three months saved give a little ground. The pension estimate, not a birthday, will tell me whether slowing down is possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if festival work never appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I save nothing from that source. I will not move rent money into a savings account just to reach five months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a paid arts-centre tutor opening posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have seen an old arts-centre tutor advert, not a current paid vacancy. I would read the real teaching qualifications and funded hours before putting its pay in our plan.

say: I would ask what **retirement really pays** before changing work.
I would say **signed theatre shows** matter before 2039 bass robots.
think: At **68**, I may still want paid bass work.
Our **three-month reserve** does not prove we can retire.
do: Request **actual pension estimate** and save 10% of extra paid festival sets after rent/food/repairs toward five months.
Keep **paid band and pupil** after 2036 while booked and until signed replacement offer.
Seek **posted bass-tutor work** after live cuts only with funded in-person hours, degree/coaching eligibility, written after-travel replacement net and bus.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about distant work while present pay and savings hold.
S4.quote: The pension estimate, not a birthday, will tell me whether slowing down is possible.
fieldNote: The **five-month goal** uses ten percent of actual extra festival fees after essentials.
The **bass-tutor job** needs funded human lessons, posted paid hours, degree/coaching eligibility, after-travel replacement pay and signed offer.

steps.text: Request actual pension estimate; keep paid band/pupil after 2036 while booked
Save 10% of extra paid festival sets after rent/food/repairs toward five months
Seek posted funded in-person bass-tutor role after live cuts if music degree/coaching qualify and bus fits
Require written net after travel replacing losses; keep band until signed offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because guide orders could stop before a paid new seat opens. Signed shows, an actual pension estimate and a posted role with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the last bus does to a musician’s options. A paid job across town is only a real option if I can get home after the curtain falls.

headlineQuote: A paid job across town is only a real option if I can get home after the curtain falls.
portrait: At **58**, Gareth is an experienced theatre bassist with a music degree, partner, grown children and three months saved.
His **typical pay** comes from pit shows, guide grooves and one pupil, with some other theatres nearby.
He uses **AI occasionally** for set lists and would learn a new timing checker only on controlled owned music.
He considers **paid amplifier repair training** only with recognized qualification, funded tuition and protected show wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove a fifth of Gareth’s pay from rehearsal-guide recordings.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed theatre shows**, actual pension figures and a posted role with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
